//autoClosingPairs: Typing `{-` gives `{- | -}`, the caret before the space. `{` auto-closes first, to
`{|}`; at the `-`, VS Code (and Monaco) find the longer `{-` pair, see that the `}`
already after the caret is the close of the `{` pair it contains, and insert only
the rest of ` -}` (`_findContainedAutoClosingPair` in the editor's
cursorTypeEditOperations), so nothing is stranded. Leaving the pair out would be
worse than in the `(* *)` era this note used to defend: `{` then `-` would leave
`{-}`, which spec/comments.md §3 reads as an *unterminated* comment, and the rest
of the file would paint as one. One more `-` gives `{--| -}`, the doc opener, since
no pair ends in `-` after `{-`. The space in the close is the `{- note -}` house
spelling, as JavaScript's `/**` pair closes with ` */`. Not in strings or comments:
inside a block comment a nested `{-` is legal but usually commented-out code being
typed over, and in a line comment it is prose.
The `${-` pair is a shim for the one place `{-` is not a comment: spec/comments.md
§3 gives the `{` of an interpolation's `${` to the string, so `"${-x}"` interpolates
`-x`. The editor takes the longest matching open, so at `${` the shim wins over
`{-`; its close is exactly the `{` pair's `}`, which the containment rule above
then subtracts, so typing the `-` inserts nothing else — `"${-|}"`, as if neither
pair existed. Without it the hole would gain ` -}` mid-expression.
//wordPattern: The object form is required, not a bare string: VS Code compiles a string
wordPattern with no flags, and without `u` every `\p{...}` degrades into an
identity escape — the class silently becomes the literal set `p{IDStart}$_`,
so double-clicking `map` would select `ap` and `xs` would select nothing.
The repertoire itself is spec/lexer.md §3.1's ECMAScript ID_Start/ID_Continue.

//: Hexagon is layout-sensitive: a block opens by indenting under its header.
A header ending in `=` already covers `constraint C<a> =` and `honor C<T> =`,
and leaves `honor C<T> = derive` alone — spec/lexer.md §4.1 makes that a
complete one-line declaration that opens no block.
The scrutinee-taking forms open their block from the *front* of the line, not
the end: `match next(current)` and `while searching` are followed by an
indented block, and `let first(v) = match v` puts `match` mid-line, so those
words are matched wherever they appear rather than only at end of line.
`extern from` is the one block header that does neither.
Lay out a doc comment the way spec/doc-comments.md §3.1 writes its multi-line
body: Enter on a line that *opens* a doc comment and leaves it open indents the
next line one level under the opener, and when the auto-closed ` -}` is right
after the caret it goes to a line of its own at the opener's column — so `{--|
-}` becomes the newline-first idiom, `{--` / indented body / `-}`. Lines inside
the body keep their indentation by VS Code's default, which is all the body needs;
the old rules' ` * ` continuation was OCaml's and JSDoc's convention, and §3.1's
dedent would keep a typed star as content, a stray Markdown list marker.
The opener they recognize is spec/doc-comments.md §2.1's, the same `(?![-}])`
predicate the grammar uses: §2.2's carve-outs, the empty block comment `{--}` and
the banner openers `{---`, `{----…`, are not doc comments and are not laid out as
ones, and neither is `{-|`. A line comment is never documentation (§2.3), so no
rule continues a `--` or `---` run.
